mcqs.q: Necrosis is defined as:
opts: Local death of a large group of cells within the living body
mcqs.explain: Necrosis is the local death of a large group of cells in the living body, with swelling, membrane rupture, leakage of contents and inflammation.

mcqs.q: The nuclear changes seen in necrosis are:
mcqs.explain: Necrotic nuclei undergo pyknosis (shrinkage), karyorrhexis (fragmentation) and karyolysis (dissolution).

mcqs.q: The MOST common type of necrosis, caused by a sudden cut-off of blood supply, is:
mcqs.explain: Coagulative necrosis is the most common type, caused by ischaemia; it occurs in all organs except the brain, preserving tissue architecture.

mcqs.q: Coagulative necrosis occurs in all organs EXCEPT the:
mcqs.explain: Coagulative necrosis occurs in all organs except the brain; the brain (CNS) undergoes liquefactive necrosis instead.

mcqs.q: Liquefactive necrosis, producing creamy yellow pus, occurs in the:
mcqs.explain: Liquefactive necrosis digests dead cells into a viscous liquid (pus); it is typical of the CNS and of bacterial/fungal abscesses.

mcqs.q: Caseation (cheese-like) necrosis is characteristically caused by:
mcqs.explain: Caseation necrosis (friable, white, cheese-like) is characteristic of tuberculosis; microscopically there is structureless pink material.

mcqs.q: Fat necrosis classically occurs in:
mcqs.explain: Fat necrosis is enzymatic (acute pancreatitis releases enzymes that liquefy fat) or traumatic (e.g. breast trauma rupturing fat cells).

mcqs.q: Fibrinoid necrosis, showing pink fibrin-like material in vessel walls, is seen in:
mcqs.explain: Fibrinoid necrosis deposits pink fibrin-like material in the walls of arteries, typically in vasculitis/autoimmune disease.

mcqs.q: Apoptosis is:
opts: Programmed death of single cells or small groups, forming apoptotic bodies
Death of large groups of cells with inflammation
mcqs.explain: Apoptosis is programmed cell death of single cells/small groups; the cell shrinks and breaks into apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed.

mcqs.q: Which is a PHYSIOLOGICAL cause of apoptosis?
opts: Embryogenesis and removal of self-reactive lymphocytes
mcqs.explain: Physiological apoptosis eliminates cells no longer needed — during embryogenesis, neutrophils after inflammation, and self-reactive lymphocytes.

mcqs.q: A PATHOLOGICAL trigger of apoptosis is:
opts: DNA damage from radiation/anticancer drugs or viral infection (HIV)
mcqs.explain: Pathological apoptosis follows DNA damage (radiation, cytotoxic drugs) or viral infection (e.g. HIV).

mcqs.q: Regarding cell size, which is correct?
mcqs.explain: In necrosis cells swell (enlarge); in apoptosis they shrink (reduce in size).

mcqs.q: Regarding the plasma membrane and inflammation:
opts: Necrosis disrupts the membrane and causes inflammation; apoptosis keeps it intact with no inflammation
mcqs.explain: In necrosis the membrane is disrupted and contents leak out, provoking inflammation; in apoptosis the membrane stays intact (contents in apoptotic bodies) with no inflammation.

mcqs.q: Gangrene is defined as:
opts: Massive tissue necrosis followed by putrefaction
mcqs.explain: Gangrene is massive tissue necrosis followed by putrefaction by saprophytic bacteria.

mcqs.q: Gangrenous tissue turns BLACK because:
opts: Hydrogen sulphide combines with haemoglobin iron to form iron sulphide
mcqs.explain: Saprophytic bacteria liberate H₂S, which combines with the iron of haemoglobin to form iron sulphide, staining the tissue black.

mcqs.q: Dry gangrene occurs in parts that are:
opts: Poor in blood supply and tissue fluids
mcqs.explain: Dry gangrene occurs in parts poor in blood supply and tissue fluids (e.g. the extremities/toes).

mcqs.q: Moist gangrene occurs in parts that are:
mcqs.explain: Moist gangrene develops in parts rich in tissue fluids (e.g. bowel, internal organs), where bacterial growth is rapid.

mcqs.q: On microscopy, the cytoplasm of a necrotic cell typically appears:
mcqs.explain: Necrotic cytoplasm becomes eosinophilic (red) with an indistinct cell membrane.

mcqs.q: In coagulative necrosis, the dead tissue:
opts: Preserves its architecture for some days with no cell details
mcqs.explain: Coagulative necrosis preserves the tissue's gross architecture for at least some days, though individual cell details are lost (firm, opaque white).

mcqs.q: In apoptosis, the cellular contents are:
opts: Released within membrane-bound apoptotic bodies (no leakage)
mcqs.explain: Apoptotic cells fragment into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed (usually by macrophages) without leaking contents or inflammation.

mcqs.q: Which form of cell death can be PHYSIOLOGICAL (normal)?
mcqs.explain: Apoptosis can be physiologic or pathologic; necrosis (and gangrene) are always pathologic.

mcqs.q: Putrefaction in gangrene is caused by:
opts: Saprophytic bacteria breaking down protein, releasing H₂S (foul odour)
mcqs.explain: Saprophytic bacteria break down the protein of necrotic tissue, liberating hydrogen sulphide that gives the foul odour.

mcqs.q: The two forms of IRREVERSIBLE cell injury are:
mcqs.explain: Irreversible cell injury (cell death) has two forms: necrosis and apoptosis.

saqs.q: Define necrosis and give its nuclear changes.
saqs.a: Local death of a large group of cells in the living body (swelling, membrane rupture, inflammation). Nuclear changes: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis.

saqs.q: List the types of necrosis with a cause/site for each.
Define apoptosis and give a physiological and a pathological cause.
saqs.a: Programmed death of single/small groups of cells forming apoptotic bodies. Physiologic: embryogenesis; pathologic: DNA damage (radiation/HIV).

saqs.q: Compare necrosis and apoptosis (size, membrane, inflammation).
saqs.a: Necrosis: enlarged, membrane disrupted, contents leak, inflammation present. Apoptosis: shrunken, membrane intact, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation.

saqs.q: Define gangrene and explain why it turns black.
saqs.a: Massive tissue necrosis + putrefaction. It turns black because H₂S combines with haemoglobin iron to form iron sulphide.
Dry gangrene: in parts poor in blood supply/tissue fluids. Moist gangrene: in parts rich in tissue fluids.
Occurs in acute pancreatitis: released pancreatic enzymes liquefy fat cells in the peritoneal cavity.
